Family system theories suggest that the interparental relationship is key for other relationships within the family, including those in individual mother- and father-child dyads. Few studies, however, have elucidated how the legacy of parents' attachment security unfolds through family relationships to child outcomes. We test a developmental longitudinal cascade, conceptualized as a sequential mediation model, from parents' attachment security, assessed as their secure base script knowledge when children were infants, to their self-reported interparental relationship quality at toddler age, to their observed relationships with their children at age 3 years, and, ultimately, to children's developmental outcomes at age 4.5 years (self-regulation and moral self). We leverage multimethod data (interviews, reports, observations) from a study of 200 community families in the U.S. Midwest (mothers, fathers, and children). We adopt recent perspectives that emphasize positive socialization processes and successful outcomes rather than detrimental pathways conferring risks. In analyses that controlled for the continuity of interparental and parent-child relationships, we supported several mediational paths. Results for mother-child dyads supported the entire hypothesized longitudinal sequence from mothers' attachment security to the mother-child relationship to children's positive developmental outcomes. For father-child dyads, that key cascade was not supported. However, several shorter alternative indirect paths were found in both dyads. title: Changing speed along the mental line: A SNARC-like effect for visual acceleration
abstract: Abstract Humans tend to map magnitudes onto space, with smaller values associated with the left and larger values with the right. Recent evidence suggests that such spatial mappings extend beyond numbers to include visual speed. Whether a second-order motion property, such as visual acceleration, is also spatially represented remains unclear. We addressed this question in two experiments using a centrally presented random dot kinematogram (RDK). Participants indicated, via lateralised key presses, whether the stimulus decelerated or accelerated relative to an initial constant-speed reference. In Experiment 1, all dots moved coherently in a single direction randomly selected on each trial. In Experiment 2, dot directions were randomised at the element level, creating an isotropic motion field. A distance effect (i.e., faster responses for larger absolute acceleration values) emerged in both experiments, indicating that acceleration was processed as a continuous magnitude. Crucially, a left-to-right spatial mapping emerged only in Experiment 2. These findings provide evidence that visual acceleration can be spatially represented, but that this mapping depends on the structure of the motion signal.

title: Effect of Network Structure on the Spread of Linguistic Behavior
abstract: Abstract Theoretical and computational models predict that social‐network topology shapes the diffusion of linguistic forms, yet direct experimental evidence remains limited. Across three laboratory experiments, we tested whether network structure or seed placement influences the spread of target lexical items, while holding task demands constant. Experiment 1 compared clustered (high‐transitivity) and random (low‐transitivity) 12‐node networks ( N = 120). Experiment 2 extended this design to larger 24‐node networks ( N = 240). Experiment 3 provided an exploratory follow‐up on seed placement within clustered networks, seeding either a dense local cluster or evenly spaced nodes ( N = 120). In each study, participants engaged in dyadic problem‐solving and image‐description tasks while confederates covertly introduced target lexical items (e.g., antennae ) to initiate diffusion. Lexical adoption was measured as the proportion of naming choices containing the target words, and lexical diversity was indexed using type–token ratio (TTR) across interaction rounds. Across all conditions, TTR declined linearly over time, indicating convergence on previously produced lexical items. Mixed effects logistic regression revealed no reliable differences in adoption between clustered and random network topologies or between seed‐placement conditions. Together, these results suggest that, under the present conditions, lexical diffusion in small networks engaged in dyadic problem‐solving is largely insensitive to global network structure or seed configuration. The findings identify boundary conditions on network effects in lexical alignment and highlight the need for richer interactional contexts and larger‐scale networks in future experimental work.

title: Why are pictures remembered better than sounds? The roles of subjective vividness of mental imagery and semantic labels
A match made in mental space: Alignment between target skew and cue organization influences recall of attribute values
abstract: Abstract Recall is often more successful for items from sparse (distinct) regions and less successful from dense (less distinct) regions in memory space. We propose that retrieval cues are also organized into crowded and less crowded regions depending on distinctiveness, and that successful retrieval depends on the distributional match between the organization of targets and cues. As a real-world test case, we used the labels from the European Union’s old (A+++, A++, A+, A, B, C, D) and new (A, B, C, D, E, F, G) energy-label scale as cues for memory retrieval of appliances’ kilowatt-hour (kWh) values. In a preregistered experiment, participants rated seven refrigerators, while studying associated kWh values drawn from a positive, a negative, or a non-skewed distribution. Ratings confirmed that the labels of the old scale were psychologically skewed in mental space whereas the new scale had a more linear organization. After a brief filled delay, labels served as retrieval cues for kWh recall. Analyses of recall patterns, complemented by analyses of recall error, showed that the linear cue scale yielded recalled values that were closer to the correct kWh values when target values were non-skewed, but recalled values were overly linear when targets were skewed. Conversely, recall was most successful with the skewed cue scale when target values were positively skewed. These findings suggest that retrieval cues constrain reconstruction by imposing a distributional structure on target representations, and that recall is most successful when this structure aligns with the organization of encoded values in mental space.

title: From faux flipped to gamified flipped classrooms: scaffolding and cognitive load management
abstract: Background Students new to flipped classrooms frequently encounter challenges with motivation and comprehension when engaging with pre-class materials independently, particularly outside scheduled class hours. Aims This study examined a scaffolded flipped-learning approach that helped students move step by step from a Faux Flipped Classroom (FFC) to a Regular Flipped Classroom (RFC), and then to a Gamified Flipped Classroom (GFC) over one semester. The goal was to support students in adapting to flipped learning, managing their mental workload, and improving their learning performance. Method Mixed methods were employed in the data collection. For quantitative data, learning achievement was assessed with tests and self-rating scales measured cognitive load, while qualitative interviews provided more detailed feedback. Results The results revealed that students in the experimental group who learned through the scaffolding strategy performed better than their counterparts in the control group. Meanwhile, both groups demonstrated a small drop in intrinsic cognitive load, likely because they became more familiar with the tasks rather than because the material got easier. However, the scaffolded group showed a larger drop in unnecessary cognitive load and a larger increase in germane cognitive effort, suggesting the intervention helped students focus more on learning and less on confusion or figuring out what to do. Intrinsic and germane cognitive load should be interpreted cautiously because they are closely related. Conclusion This study contributes to Cognitive Load Theory and scaffolding research by showing that flipped classroom success depends not only on design but also on how students are gradually prepared to use it.

title: One, Two, Three, Four… What's More? Successor Relations, not Mappings to Approximate Magnitudes, Support Learning the Later‐Greater Principle
abstract: Abstract As we count up, number words that occur later in our count denote greater quantities. Here, we tested whether children's understanding of this “later‐greater” principle originates from associating number words with approximate magnitudes, or if instead it arises from knowledge of successor relations between individual number words. In Experiment 1 ( N = 60), we found that children can identify the greater of two small number words (e.g., “six” vs. “ten”) based on associative mappings between number words and the ANS but do not rely on such mappings to compare larger numbers (e.g., “twenty‐four” vs. “twenty‐six”). In Experiment 2 ( N = 60), we replicate these findings and show that children's knowledge of successor relations between number words predicts later‐greater knowledge, while mappings to the ANS do not. We conclude that children's knowledge of successor relations, but not associative mappings to approximate magnitudes, are implicated in learning the later‐greater principle.
